# Data and scope {#sec-data}

<!-- Data and feature set are identical to paper 2a. This section provides
     a brief pointer to paper 2a §2 rather than repeating the full data
     description. The only new element is the market baseline construction
     (discounted Harville). -->

The data, the race-selection rules, the train/test split and the feature
set are identical to paper 2a; we refer the reader there (paper 2a, §2)
rather than repeat them. The one genuinely new ingredient this paper needs
is a *place-market* baseline, constructed below.

## Market baseline: discounted Harville

The win-market baseline used in papers 1 and 2a — starting-price implied
win probability, over-round adjusted — cannot be directly applied to a
top-3 ranking objective. We require market-implied *place* probabilities
for each horse.

We derive these from win starting prices using the discounted Harville
formula [@lobaconshone1994; @lobaconshone2008]. Under pure Harville
[@harville1973], the probability that horse $j$ finishes second given
horse $i$ won is $p_j / (1 - p_i)$, where $p_k$ denotes win probability.
The probability of a specific top-2 order $(i, j)$ is then
$p_i\, p_j / (1 - p_i)$, and so on for deeper rankings. Pure Harville is
mathematically equivalent to the Plackett–Luce model: comparing a
PL-fitted model against a pure-Harville market baseline would be circular,
since both share the same functional form.

Lo & Bacon-Shone show that pure Harville systematically overestimates
place probabilities for favourites and underestimates them for
longer-priced horses — the favourite–longshot bias operating in the place
dimension. The discounted Harville corrects this by replacing $p_k$ with
$p_k^{\alpha}$ in the Harville formula, with $\alpha < 1$ applied to the
2nd-place conditional and a smaller $\alpha$ to the 3rd-place conditional.
We use $\alpha = 0.80$ for 2nd place and $\alpha = 0.65$ for 3rd place,
following Lo & Bacon-Shone's recommended values when
starting-price-derived probabilities are used as inputs. The discounting
breaks the PL equivalence and corrects the favourite bias, giving a
non-trivial market baseline against which the feature-based exploded model
can be evaluated.
